segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying is this: as long as the heir is a minor, he is no different from a slave, though he is owner of everything,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also we, when we were minors, were enslaved under the elements of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the fullness of time came, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And because you are sons, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Abba, Father!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then also an heir through God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But back then, not knowing God, you were slaves to those that by nature are not gods.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God—how can you turn back again to the weak and destitute elements? Do you want to be slaves to them all over again?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are observing days and months and seasons and years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am afraid for you, that perhaps I have labored over you for nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Become as I am, because I also became as you are—brothers and sisters, I beg you. You did me no wrong.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You know that it was because of a bodily illness that I first announced the good news to you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and what was a trial to you in my body you did not scorn or spit at; rather, you welcomed me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where then is that blessedness of yours? For I testify to you that, had it been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They are courting you, but not for good; no, they want to shut you out, so that you will court them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it is good to be courted in a good cause at all times, and not only when I am present with you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: my children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am at a loss about you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not listen to the Law?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through a promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These things are said allegorically, for these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Rejoice, barren woman who bears no children; break out and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the deserted woman are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now you, brothers and sisters, are children of promise, like Isaac.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now also.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But what does the Scripture say?

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will never inherit with the son of the free woman.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.

notes.traditional: elements of the world; elemental spirits; elementary principles
notes.note: The Greek word could mean the basic components of something: the letters of the alphabet, the rudiments of a subject, or the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made. In the period, the full phrase “elements of the world” most often refers to those physical elements, which many peoples revered as divine. Other interpreters take it here as “elementary principles” of religion, or as “elemental spirits,” a sense not clearly attested this early. The plain rendering leaves these options open; the same word recurs in verse 9.

notes.traditional: adoption of sons; adoption as sons
notes.note: The word is the ordinary Greek legal term for adoption, a practice familiar in the Roman world, where an adopted son gained full rights of inheritance. “Sons” is kept because the argument turns on inheritance and on the link with God’s own Son; Paul has just said (3:28) that this status belongs to men and women alike.
“Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in address within the family and in prayer. Paul keeps the Aramaic word and sets its Greek equivalent beside it, as also in Romans 8:15 and Mark 14:36.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The verb was an ordinary word for bringing or proclaiming good news, used also of public and imperial announcements. “Preach the gospel” has become a purely religious phrase in English, so the plainer rendering is used here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The Greek expression can mean “the first time,” which would imply Paul had visited the Galatians twice before writing, or simply “originally, back then.” The second, looser sense was common in the period, and the rendering here does not press the first. The question bears on dating the letter and remains disputed.

The word means a putting to the proof; here Paul’s illness was a hardship that tested how the Galatians would receive him, so “trial” is used and not the older “temptation.” Most modern versions agree. Some manuscripts read “my trial” for “your trial,” which lies behind the King James wording “my temptation which was in my flesh.”

The verb literally means to spit out. Spitting was a common gesture for warding off illness, the evil eye or a demonic influence at the sight of a sick person, and it could also simply express disgust. Many translations paraphrase with “reject” or “loathe”; the literal gesture is kept here because ancient readers would have recognized it.

notes.traditional: zealously affect; make much of; are zealous for
notes.note: The verb means to be eagerly devoted to someone or to seek them earnestly, whether honorably or not. Paul uses it three times across verses 17 and 18, and “court” is used each time so the repetition can be heard. Other versions have “make much of” or “are zealous to win you over.”

Paul uses the same Greek word twice with a shift of reference. The first means the law of Moses as a regime of commandments; the second means the Law as Scripture, the five books of Moses, from which the Genesis story of Abraham’s two sons is drawn. The capital letter marks the second sense.

The verb can mean either to speak allegorically or to interpret allegorically. Paul may be saying that the Genesis narrative itself points to something further, or that he is now reading it in a figurative way; the Greek allows both. He does not deny that the events happened. He finds in the two women a pattern for two covenants.

notes.phrase: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
notes.traditional: For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia
notes.note: The manuscripts differ here. Some omit the name Hagar and read “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia.” The reading translated here identifies Hagar with Sinai, the place where the law was given; scholars are divided over which form is original.

Genesis 21:9 says only that Sarah saw Ishmael “playing” or “laughing,” in the Greek version “playing with Isaac her son.” Jewish interpretive tradition took this as mockery or hostility toward Isaac, and Paul reflects that reading. He sees the same pattern in the pressure his converts now face.

candidates.reason: Occurs in Galatians, Colossians, Hebrews and 2 Peter, and translations diverge sharply (elements, elemental spirits, basic principles), so readers will be confused if it varies.
The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and needs one policy on “brothers” versus “brothers and sisters.”
Paul’s uses range from the physical body to human nature opposed to the Spirit, and translations vary widely between “flesh,” “body,” “human nature” and “sinful nature.”
Recurs across the whole New Testament, and translations alternate between “slave,” “servant” and “bondservant,” which obscures the social reality and Paul’s slavery metaphors.
Used in Romans, Galatians and Ephesians, where translations vary between “adoption,” “adoption as sons,” “adoption as children” and “sonship.”
